title: Generative AI Tools
description: Seven tools, what each is genuinely good at, and where each one falls short.

lessons.title: ChatGPT
lessons.description: The sensible default, and the ten minutes of setup most people skip.
lessons.content:
> These tools change constantly. Features arrive, limits move, and tiers are renamed. This lesson covers what each tool is **for**, which stays stable. Check the current features yourself before relying on any specific capability.

## Learn

ChatGPT, from OpenAI, is the tool that made this technology mainstream. For most people it is the default, and for good reason: it does most things competently and has the largest surrounding ecosystem.

### What it does

General-purpose assistance: writing, explaining, analysing, coding, summarising. It handles images as input, generates images, runs code to answer questions, searches the web, and reads files you upload.

The custom instructions feature is worth finding on day one. It lets you set standing preferences that apply to every conversation -- your role, your writing preferences, how much detail you want. That is a system prompt in the sense of module 4, and setting it well improves every subsequent conversation.

### When to use it

**As your default** when you have no specific reason to use something else. It is rarely the wrong choice.

**When you want one tool for many things** rather than switching between specialists.

**When you need the ecosystem.** Its integrations and third-party connections are the most extensive, which matters if you want to plug it into other software.

**When you want something built on it.** Custom assistants configured for a specific task, shared with a team, are straightforward here.

## Demonstrate

A task that shows the breadth. Take a spreadsheet of any real data you have -- expenses, marks, survey responses -- and upload it.

Then ask, in sequence, in one conversation:

1. *"What is in this file? Describe the columns and how many rows."*
2. *"What are the three most notable patterns? Quote the figures."*
3. *"Make a chart showing the most important one."*
4. *"Write two sentences I could put in an email summarising this for my manager."*

Notice what happened: it read a file, analysed it, ran code to produce a chart, and wrote prose, without you changing tools or explaining the data again. That continuity across different kinds of work is the thing it is best at.

## Limitations

**It is confident when it should not be.** Its default register is assured. Module 3's defences apply in full.

**Web search results vary in quality.** When it searches, check the sources, especially for anything current or contested.

**It has a tendency to agree.** Push back on a correct answer and it will often fold. Do not treat agreement as confirmation.

**Its analysis of data is only as good as its reading of your file.** Check that it parsed the columns as you expected before trusting anything downstream.

**Free tiers change.** What is available without paying moves regularly. Check rather than assume.

## Practice

Set your custom instructions properly. Include who you are, what you usually need help with, and how you want responses formatted -- length, level of detail, whether you want caveats.

Then ask the same question before and after, in two fresh conversations. Record the difference.

Most people find this the highest-value ten minutes they spend on any of these tools, and most people have never done it.

## What to remember

- The sensible default: broad, capable, with the largest ecosystem
- Set custom instructions once and every conversation improves
- Strong at carrying one piece of work across files, analysis, charts and prose
- Confident by default, and inclined to agree when challenged
- Check the sources whenever it searches

lessons.title: Google Gemini
lessons.description: Multimodal by design, and wired into the products you may already use.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

Gemini, from Google, was built for more than text from the start, and it lives inside the Google products many people already use all day.

### What it does

General assistance, like the others, with two distinguishing emphases: **multimodal work** and **integration with Google's own products**.

If your documents are in Google Docs, your mail is in Gmail and your files are in Drive, having an assistant that can reach them directly removes a great deal of copying and pasting.

It also handles long inputs well, which matters when you want to work with a whole document rather than an extract.

### When to use it

**When your work already lives in Google's products.** The integration is the reason to choose it, and it is a good one.

**For image and video understanding.** Ask questions about what is in a picture, a diagram, a screenshot or a recording.

**For long documents.** Where you want the whole thing considered rather than a chunk.

**When you want its answer alongside a web search**, since search is where Google starts from.

## Demonstrate

The integration is best seen rather than described. If you have a Google account:

1. Find a long document in your Drive -- a report, a set of notes, a policy
2. Ask Gemini to summarise it **by name**, without copying anything in
3. Ask a follow-up about a specific section
4. Ask it to draft an email about the document

The absence of copying and pasting is the point. For people whose working life is in these products, that friction removal changes how often they actually use the tool.

If you do not use Google products, do the multimodal demonstration instead: give it a photograph of a page of handwritten notes and ask for a typed, structured version.

## Limitations

**The integration cuts both ways.** An assistant that can read your mail and files is one you should think about before enabling at work. Check what your organisation permits.

**Multimodal is strong on meaning, weak on precision.** As module 3 covered: excellent at describing a chart, unreliable at reading a value off it.

**Behaviour differs between surfaces.** The same underlying family behaves differently in the standalone app, in Docs, and in Search. Do not assume what worked in one works identically in another.

**Long input is not the same as long attention.** A model that accepts a long document does not necessarily weight every part of it equally. For a detail that matters, point at it rather than trusting it was noticed.

## Practice

If you use Google products: pick one recurring task involving a document or an email and do it through Gemini instead of manually. Record how long each took.

If you do not: give it three images of increasing difficulty -- a clear diagram, a photograph of handwriting, and a dense chart -- and ask a specific question about each. Record where the quality drops off.

## What to remember

- Built multimodal, and integrated with Google's own products
- The integration is the main reason to choose it
- Strong on long inputs, but point at the detail that matters
- Meaning yes, precision no, on anything visual
- Think about permissions before connecting an assistant to your mail and files

lessons.title: Microsoft Copilot
lessons.description: One name, several products; the 365 integration is the distinctive one.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

Microsoft Copilot is the same general capability, placed inside Microsoft's products. The name covers several things, which causes confusion worth clearing up.

### What it does

**Copilot as a chat assistant** is a general-purpose tool like the others.

**Copilot inside Microsoft 365** is the interesting one. It appears in Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams, and works on the document, spreadsheet, deck or thread you have open.

**GitHub Copilot** is a different product for writing code. It has its own lesson later in this module. Despite sharing a name, do not conflate them.

### When to use it

**When your work is in Microsoft 365.** This is the whole case for it. Drafting in Word, analysing in Excel, building a deck in PowerPoint, catching up on a Teams meeting you missed.

**For meeting summaries.** If your organisation runs meetings in Teams, having them summarised with action items attributed to people is genuinely one of the strongest practical uses of AI available today.

**When organisational data is the context.** In a corporate setting it can draw on your organisation's own documents, which is a real advantage over a tool that knows nothing about your company.

## Demonstrate

The Excel case shows the shape best. Open a spreadsheet with real data and ask, in plain language:

- *"Which region had the largest drop between the first and last month?"*
- *"Add a column showing month-on-month change as a percentage."*
- *"Make a chart showing the trend for the three largest regions."*

You are describing outcomes rather than writing formulas. For people who use spreadsheets constantly and have never learned the formula language properly, this is a large change.

The same shape applies elsewhere: describe the outcome, in the application, on the document you already have open.

## Limitations

**The name means several products.** Be precise about which one you are discussing, especially when reading advice online.

**Availability depends on your organisation.** The 365 features are licensed, and whether you have them is an administrator's decision, not yours.

**It sees what you have access to.** Useful, and also a reason to think carefully in a workplace. It can surface things from documents you had forgotten you could see.

**Spreadsheet results still need checking.** It produces a formula or a figure; it does not guarantee the figure is right. Check against something you know.

**Meeting summaries miss nuance.** They capture what was said. They do not capture that the room went quiet, or that the agreement was reluctant. Do not treat a summary as the full record of a meeting that mattered.

## Practice

If you have 365 Copilot: take your longest recent Teams meeting and ask for a summary with action items. Then check it against your own memory or notes. Record what it captured and what it missed.

If you do not: use the chat version on a document you paste in, asking for the same -- summary, decisions, actions with owners. The checking exercise is the valuable part either way.

## What to remember

- One name, several products -- the 365 integration is the distinctive one
- Describing outcomes instead of writing formulas is a real change for spreadsheet users
- Meeting summaries with attributed actions are among the strongest everyday uses
- Availability is decided by your organisation, not by you
- It captures what was said, not what was meant

lessons.title: Claude
lessons.description: Long-form work, and an assistant more willing to say it is unsure.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

Claude, from Anthropic, is a general-purpose assistant with a noticeably different character from the others.

### What it does

The usual range: writing, analysis, coding, summarising, reading documents and images. Where it stands out in practice is **long-form work** -- extended writing, analysis of long documents, and multi-file coding -- and in how it behaves when it is uncertain.

Anthropic is a company founded with an explicit focus on AI safety, and that shows up in the product. Claude is more likely than some to say it is not sure, to note a caveat, and to push back on a request it thinks is unwise.

### When to use it

**For long-form writing and editing.** Reports, essays, documentation, long-form analysis.

**For working through a long document carefully.** Where you want engagement with the detail rather than a summary.

**For coding**, particularly where the change spans several files or the problem needs to be understood before it is solved.

**When you want to be told about uncertainty.** If you would rather hear "the document does not say" than a confident guess, this tendency is useful.

## Demonstrate

The character difference shows up best on a question with no clean answer.

Ask several tools the same genuinely contested question from your own field -- something where experts disagree. Not a factual lookup; a judgement.

Compare how each handles the disagreement. Some produce a confident synthesis that reads as settled. You will generally find Claude more likely to lay out the positions and say which parts are unresolved.

Which you prefer is a genuine matter of taste and task. For a first draft you will edit, confidence is efficient. For understanding a field you are new to, being told what is unsettled is more useful than being told a tidy answer.

## Limitations

**The caution can be excessive.** It sometimes hedges where a direct answer would serve better, and sometimes declines things that were fine. If you get a refusal you think is wrong, explaining the actual context often resolves it.

**It hallucinates.** Being more willing to express uncertainty is not the same as being immune. Every defence from module 3 still applies.

**Fewer integrations than some.** If you need an assistant wired into many other systems, others have a longer head start.

**Specifics change.** Everything about which model is current, what it costs and what it can process is exactly the kind of claim this course refuses to state, because it would be wrong by the time you read it.

## Practice

Take a question from your field where knowledgeable people genuinely disagree.

Ask it in three different tools. For each answer, mark: does it acknowledge the disagreement, does it name the positions, does it state which parts are unresolved, or does it produce a single confident answer?

Then decide which behaviour you want for which kind of task. Most people conclude they want confidence for drafting and caution for understanding, and that is a perfectly good conclusion to reach deliberately rather than by accident.

## What to remember

- Anthropic's assistant, with an explicit safety emphasis that shows in its behaviour
- Strong on long-form writing, careful document work and multi-file coding
- More likely to express uncertainty and push back, which suits some tasks and not others
- The caution is occasionally excessive; supplying real context usually helps
- Willingness to say "I am not sure" is not immunity from hallucination

lessons.title: Perplexity
lessons.description: Search with citations, and why the citations only help if you click them.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

Perplexity is a different shape from the others. It is built around **search with citations**, rather than being a general assistant that happens to be able to search.

### What it does

You ask a question. It searches, reads what it finds, and answers with numbered citations to the sources it used. You can click each one.

That last part is the whole product. The difference between "here is an answer" and "here is an answer, and here is exactly where each part came from" is the difference between something you must verify from scratch and something you can check in a minute.

### When to use it

**For anything current.** Recent events, current prices, what a company announced last week.

**For research where you need sources.** When you will have to cite something, or convince someone, or check it later.

**As a starting point for reading.** Often the most valuable output is not the answer but the list of sources, which gives you a reading list on an unfamiliar topic in seconds.

**When you do not trust an answer and want to see the working.** Ask the same question here and follow the citations.

## Demonstrate

Take a question where you already know the answer well -- something from your own field or your own life.

Ask it. Then do two things:

1. Judge the answer against what you know
2. **Click every citation** and judge the sources as sources

The second is the exercise. You will often find the answer is broadly right and one of the sources is a marketing page, a forum post, or an article that says something slightly different from what was attributed to it.

That is not a criticism of the tool specifically -- it is what search returns. But it is the habit worth building: **the citations make checking possible, and they only help if you actually check**.

## Limitations

**A citation is not a guarantee.** It shows where the claim came from, not that the source is good or that it was read correctly. Both failure modes happen.

**It is only as good as what it found.** A poorly-covered topic gives a poor answer assembled from poor sources, delivered in the same confident format as a well-sourced one.

**It is weaker as a general assistant.** For drafting, long-form writing, coding and open-ended thinking, the general-purpose tools are better. Use it for what it is.

**Recency is not accuracy.** The most recent source is not necessarily the most reliable one, and search tends to favour recent.

## Practice

Pick three questions: one you know the answer to, one where you do not, and one about something from the last two weeks.

Ask all three. For each, click every citation and grade the sources: would you cite this yourself, yes or no?

Record your hit rate. Most people find it is high but not perfect, and that the misses cluster on the question where they had no prior knowledge -- which is exactly where they would have been fooled.

## What to remember

- Built around search with clickable citations, not a general assistant
- Best for current information and anything you will need to cite
- The source list is often more valuable than the answer
- Citations make checking possible; they do not replace it
- Only as good as what the search returned, and it looks the same either way

lessons.title: NotebookLM
lessons.description: Answers only from your own sources, and declines what they do not cover.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

NotebookLM, from Google, is built on a single constraint that makes it unusually trustworthy: **it only answers from sources you give it**.

You upload documents -- PDFs, notes, slides, links, transcripts -- and it answers questions about those, with citations pointing back to the exact passage.

### What it does

It grounds every answer in your material. Ask something the documents do not cover and it tells you, rather than filling the gap from general knowledge.

If that sounds familiar, it should: this is retrieval-augmented generation, which is module 13. NotebookLM is a polished consumer version of the thing you will build.

It also generates study aids from your sources: summaries, timelines, briefing documents, question lists, and an audio discussion of the material.

### When to use it

**Studying from a fixed set of material.** Lecture notes, a textbook chapter, a set of papers. This is the strongest use, and it is why this lesson matters for a student audience.

**Understanding a document set you did not write.** A new job's documentation, a legal agreement, a policy manual, research papers on an unfamiliar topic.

**When you need to trust the answer.** The grounding, plus citations into your own documents, makes verification fast.

**When you want the same material in a different form** -- a timeline out of a narrative, questions out of a chapter, a summary out of forty pages.

## Demonstrate

This is worth doing properly, because it is the most directly useful tool in this module for anyone studying.

1. Upload everything for one topic you are currently learning -- lecture slides, your notes, a reading, a recording transcript
2. Ask *"What are the main ideas across all of these, and where do they disagree?"*
3. Ask something specific and check the citation against the original
4. Ask something the sources genuinely do not cover, and watch it decline
5. Generate practice questions from the material and try to answer them

Step 4 is the one to pay attention to. A tool that tells you it does not know is behaving very differently from everything else in this module, and the difference is the constraint, not the intelligence.

## Limitations

**It will not go beyond your sources.** That is the feature, and it is also a limit. If your material is incomplete, so is every answer.

**It inherits your sources' errors.** Grounded in a wrong document, it gives a confidently wrong answer with a citation. Grounding is not fact-checking.

**Grounding is strong, not absolute.** It can still misread a passage or over-generalise from one. Check citations that matter.

**Generated audio and summaries are derivative.** They are a pleasant way to review material you have already engaged with, not a substitute for reading it.

## Practice

Build a notebook for something you are actually studying or need to understand. Upload at least four sources.

Then do the thing that proves the difference: ask five questions, at least two of which your sources **do not** answer.

Record how it handled the two it could not answer. Compare that behaviour with asking the same two questions in a general assistant.

Write two sentences on what the constraint bought you.

## What to remember

- Answers only from sources you provide, with citations into them
- A consumer version of RAG, which you will build in module 13
- The strongest tool here for studying a fixed set of material
- It declines what the sources do not cover, which is the whole point
- Grounding is not fact-checking: a wrong source gives a confidently wrong answer

lessons.title: GitHub Copilot
lessons.description: An in-editor coding assistant, useful even if you do not write code.
lessons.content:
> As with every tool in this module: check its current features yourself.

## Learn

GitHub Copilot is an AI assistant that lives in your code editor. Despite the shared name, it is a different product from Microsoft Copilot.

Module 9 covers AI-assisted coding properly. This lesson covers what the tool is and when it fits, so the picture of the landscape is complete.

### What it does

**Inline suggestions.** As you type, it proposes the rest of the line, the function, or the block. Press a key to accept.

**Chat in the editor.** Ask about the code you have open, with the file as context. Explain this, why does this fail, write a test for this.

**Multi-file work.** Describe a change and have it proposed across several files.

You do not have to be a programmer to benefit, which is the point most relevant to this course's audience. Reading and understanding code is a large part of what it helps with, and that is useful to anyone who occasionally has to look at a script.

### When to use it

**Writing boilerplate.** The repetitive, well-understood code that takes time and no thought.

**Working in an unfamiliar language.** You know what you want; you do not know this syntax.

**Understanding code you did not write.** Genuinely one of the strongest uses, and the most relevant to non-programmers.

**Writing tests.** Tedious, patterned, and something it does well.

**As a starting point**, always to be reviewed.

## Demonstrate

If you have an editor with it installed, do this. If not, the same exercise works by pasting code into any chat tool.

1. Find some code you did not write -- a script from a colleague, something from the internet, an example from module 2
2. Ask *"Explain what this does, line by line, to someone who does not know this language"*
3. Ask *"What could go wrong with this?"*
4. Ask *"Write a test that would catch the most likely bug"*

Step 3 is the most useful and the least used. Asking what could go wrong surfaces edge cases you would not have thought of, and it is useful even when you then disagree with the answer.

## Limitations

**It is confidently wrong in the same way as everything else.** Generated code that looks right and does not work is extremely common. Module 2's debugging exercises were not decoration.

**It suggests plausible functions that do not exist.** Particularly in less common libraries. The code fails immediately, which makes this one of the safer places for hallucination to happen.

**It does not know your intent.** It knows your code. Those are different, and a confident completion of the wrong thing is easy to accept without noticing.

**Accepting suggestions without reading is a genuine trap.** It is fast, the suggestions are usually reasonable, and the habit of accepting without reading develops quickly. Everything it writes is your responsibility.

**Think about what your code contains.** Understand what your editor sends and what your organisation permits before using it on proprietary or sensitive code.

## Practice

Take a piece of code you do not understand -- any language.

Ask for a line-by-line explanation, then ask what could go wrong, then ask for a test.

Then do the important part: **check one claim from the explanation** against documentation. Pick something specific it asserted about what a function does.

Record whether it was right. This habit -- verify one claim per explanation -- is what keeps AI-assisted coding honest.

## What to remember

- An in-editor coding assistant; not the same product as Microsoft Copilot
- Reading and explaining unfamiliar code is its most underrated use
- "What could go wrong with this?" is the best under-used question
- Generated code that looks right and fails is the normal case, not the exception
- Accepting suggestions unread is a habit that forms fast and costs later

lessons.title: Choosing between them
lessons.description: Learn one deeply, add specialists on evidence, use two for anything important.
lessons.content:
## Learn

Seven tools, considerable overlap. Here is how to decide without agonising.

### The short version

For most people, most of the time: **pick one general assistant and learn it properly**. Depth in one beats shallow familiarity with five.

Then add specialists only where a real need shows up:

- **Something current, or that you must cite** → a search-first tool like Perplexity
- **A fixed set of documents you must trust** → NotebookLM
- **Code** → an in-editor assistant like GitHub Copilot
- **Work inside Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace** → whichever matches your stack

### Choosing your general assistant

Honestly, on ordinary tasks the leading general assistants are close enough that this decision matters less than people think. Three things that legitimately decide it:

**What your organisation permits.** Often this makes the decision for you, and it is worth checking before investing time.

**Where your work already lives.** If everything is in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, the integrated option removes real friction every day.

**Which behaviour suits you.** Some tools are more confident, some more hedged; some verbose, some terse. After a week of real use you will have a preference, and it is a legitimate basis for choosing.

What should **not** decide it: benchmark scores, a comparison article, or which one someone on the internet prefers. Test on your own tasks, which is what the lab does.

### Matching tool to task

- **Draft, rewrite, explain, think out loud** -- your general assistant
- **Anything from the last few months** -- search-first, and check the sources
- **Questions about documents you hold** -- NotebookLM, or paste into a general assistant
- **Writing or understanding code** -- an in-editor assistant, or a general one for explanation
- **Spreadsheets and decks you already have open** -- whatever is integrated with them
- **A claim you will be held to** -- search-first, then verify independently

### The habit that matters more than the choice

**Use more than one for anything important.**

Ask the same question in two tools. Where they agree, your confidence should rise a little. Where they differ, you have found something worth checking -- and you would never have known from one answer.

This costs an extra minute and catches a surprising amount.

### On paying

Free tiers are enough to learn everything in this course. Whether to pay depends entirely on how often you use the tool and for what, and the offers change too often for a course to advise you. Use the free tiers until you notice a specific limit getting in your way, then decide.

## Demonstrate

The two-tool habit, made concrete.

Take a factual question in your own field where you would be embarrassed to be wrong. Ask it in two different tools, in fresh conversations.

Compare not just the conclusions but the details: numbers, names, caveats, what each said it was unsure about.

Most of the time they will agree, and that is a mildly reassuring non-event. Perhaps one time in five they will differ on something specific, and that difference is the whole value of the habit. Follow it up and see which was right.

## Practice

Write your own one-page decision guide.

List the five tasks you most often use AI for. For each, name which tool you will use and in one sentence why.

Be specific about what would make you switch. "If I need to cite it, I use a search-first tool" is a rule. "It depends" is not.

Keep it. Revisit it after the lab at the end of this module, when you have evidence rather than impressions.

## What to remember

- Learn one general assistant deeply before adding specialists
- Add a specialist when a real need appears, not in advance
- Organisational policy, your existing stack, and behaviour preference legitimately decide it
- Use two tools for anything important; disagreement is the signal
- Free tiers are enough to learn everything here

lessons.title: Practice questions and answer key
lessons.description: Ten questions covering the whole module, with a full explanation for each.
lessons.content:
Ten questions on the whole of module 5.

:::quiz
Q. What makes NotebookLM behave differently from a general assistant?
- It uses a more capable underlying model
+ It answers only from the sources you provide, and declines what they do not cover
- It has a more recent knowledge cutoff
- It is better at citations because it searches more sources
= The constraint, not the capability, is the difference. Grounding every answer in your own documents is a consumer version of retrieval-augmented generation, which module 13 covers properly.

Q. You need a fact you will be quoted on, about something that happened last month. Which approach fits best?
- A general assistant, asked to be accurate
+ A search-first tool with citations, then verify the sources independently
- NotebookLM, with the question as the only source
- Any tool, asked the same question three times
= Recent information needs search, and anything you will be held to needs sources you have actually checked. Citations make checking possible; they do not replace it.

Q. Microsoft Copilot and GitHub Copilot are:
- The same product with two names
+ Different products that share a name
- Two tiers of one subscription
- The chat and voice versions of one assistant
= Microsoft Copilot is a general assistant integrated with Microsoft 365. GitHub Copilot is a coding assistant that lives in your editor. Conflating them makes online advice about either one confusing.

Q. What is the single highest-value thing to set up in a general assistant on day one?
- The most capable model available
+ Custom instructions, so your standing preferences apply to every conversation
- Web search
- File upload permissions
= This is a system prompt in the sense of module 4. Setting who you are, what you usually need, and how you want responses formatted improves every later conversation, and most people never do it.

Q. A search-first tool gives you an answer with five citations. What is the correct posture?
- The citations mean the answer is verified
+ The citations make checking possible; click them and judge the sources
- Citations only matter for academic work
- Five citations is enough that spot-checking one is sufficient
= A citation shows where a claim came from, not that the source is good or that it was read correctly. Both failure modes are common, and they cluster on topics where you have no prior knowledge to catch them.

Q. Why is "what could go wrong with this?" a valuable question to ask a coding assistant?
- It makes the model more careful in later answers
+ It surfaces edge cases you would not have thought of, even when you disagree with some of them
- It is the only way to get the model to check its own work
- It reduces hallucination in generated code
= It is the most useful under-used question in AI-assisted coding. The value is in the cases raised, not in the model's judgement about them, which you should still apply your own thinking to.

Q. Which is a legitimate basis for choosing your main general assistant?
- Benchmark scores from a comparison article
+ What your organisation permits, where your work already lives, and which behaviour suits you
- Which one has the most parameters
- Which one was released most recently
= On ordinary tasks the leading assistants are close enough that this decision matters less than people think. Policy, existing stack and behavioural fit are real. Benchmarks and release dates are not.

Q. What is the practical value of asking the same important question in two different tools?
- It averages out the errors
+ Where they differ, you have found something specific worth checking that one answer would have hidden
- It confirms the answer when they agree
- It is faster than verifying independently
= Agreement is mildly reassuring and not proof; both can be wrong the same way. Disagreement is the actual signal, and it costs about a minute to obtain.

Q. A meeting summary tool produces action items with owners. What does it reliably fail to capture?
- Who spoke most
+ Nuance: reluctance, unspoken disagreement, the significance of a silence
- The decisions that were made
- The names of attendees
= It captures what was said, not what was meant. For a meeting that mattered, treat the summary as a record of the words and not as a full account of the room.

Q. What is the recommended approach to learning these tools?
- Learn all seven so you can pick the best one per task
+ Learn one general assistant deeply, then add specialists when a real need appears
- Use whichever is cheapest for each individual task
- Always use the most recently released tool
= Depth in one beats shallow familiarity with five. The specialists earn their place when you hit a specific need -- citations, grounded documents, code, or integration with the suite you already use.
:::

## How to read your score

Seven or more and you are ready for module 6. This module is more practical than conceptual, so if you missed questions it is usually worth going back and actually doing the demonstrations rather than rereading.

lessons.title: Hands-on lab: the same task across three tools
lessons.description: One prompt, three tools, three inputs, and a deliberate attempt to break them.
lessons.content:
Forty minutes. You will end with evidence about which tool suits your real work, rather than an opinion about which is best.

## Before you start

Pick **three** tools you can access. Any three from this module work. Each has offered a free tier; check what each currently offers.

Open all three. Have a document for recording.

## Step 1: Pick a task you actually repeat

Not a benchmark question. Something from your week.

Good choices: summarising something long for someone else; drafting a reply to a recurring kind of message; turning notes into a structured format; explaining something from your field to a beginner; checking a document against criteria.

Write the task in one sentence.

## Step 2: Write criteria before you run anything

Five criteria a good output must meet, specific enough that someone else would mark the same way.

If you have done module 4's lab, reuse that approach. "Under 200 words", "every action has an owner", "no claim that is not in the source" -- checkable things.

## Step 3: One prompt, three tools, three inputs

Write **one** prompt, using what module 4 taught: context, task, constraints, format, uncertainty instruction.

Use it unchanged in all three tools, on three real inputs. Nine runs. Fresh conversation each time.

Record every output.

## Step 4: Score

Nine outputs, five criteria. Build the grid.

Then record the things a grid does not capture:

- Which was fastest, in wall-clock seconds
- Which followed your format instruction most exactly
- Which was most verbose
- Which hedged most
- Did any invent anything? Check carefully against the source.

## Step 5: Now break them

The scores above will probably be close. Differences show at the edges, so go there. Run at least two of these across all three tools:

- **A source question.** Ask for three references on a topic in your field. Verify every one. Record which tools searched, which invented, which declined.
- **An awkward input.** Feed the same prompt an input where the right answer is "there is nothing here" -- an empty set of notes, a meeting with no decisions. Record which invent something.
- **A precision question.** Give all three a screenshot of a chart and ask for three specific values. Check them.
- **A consistency check.** Run one input three times in the same tool. Compare.

:::hint All three tools performed identically
That is a genuine and useful finding -- it means for this task, choose on speed, cost or convenience, and stop thinking about it. If you want to find a difference, the awkward input in step 5 separates tools more reliably than anything else. Most will invent something rather than report an empty result, and the ones that do not are showing you something real.
:::

## Step 6: Add a specialist

Take the same task to whichever specialist fits: a search-first tool if your task involves facts, NotebookLM if it involves a fixed document set, a coding assistant if it involves code.

Record whether the specialist beat the general assistants on your task, and by how much.

## Step 7: Write it up

1. Your task and five criteria
2. The score grid, as numbers
3. The qualitative differences
4. What happened at the edges in step 5
5. Whether the specialist earned its place
6. Which tool you will use for this task, and what would change your mind

## What good looks like

Strong write-ups quote specifics. "Tool A was better" is weak. "Tool A met 5/5 on all three inputs; Tool B dropped the owner from an action item on two of three, turning 'Ravi to book the room' into 'the room will be booked'" is strong.

Strong write-ups also report the awkward-input result honestly, including when your preferred tool was the one that invented something. That result is the most useful thing in the lab.

lessons.title: Assignment: a tool comparison for a real need
lessons.description: A recommendation a real group could adopt, marked against a published rubric.
lessons.content:
## The task

Write a **tool recommendation** for a real group of people with a real need: which AI tools they should use, for what, with the evidence and the rules that go with it.

This is a document someone could actually adopt. Write it for them, not for a marker.

## Choose a real group

Name them. Your study group, your team at work, a society committee, a department, a family business, a group of classmates.

If you genuinely cannot use a real group, invent one with specific constraints: size, what they do, what data they handle, what they are allowed to install, what they can spend.

## What to submit

One document, **1000 to 1400 words**, in six sections.

### 1. The group and their work

Who they are, what they do, and the four or five tasks where AI could genuinely help. Be specific. "They write a lot" is not a task; "they write weekly status updates summarising four project threads" is.

### 2. The constraints

At least four, each with a real basis:

- **What data is involved**, and what is not allowed to leave the organisation
- **What they are permitted to install or sign up for** -- an actual policy where one exists
- **What they can spend**, if anything
- **What skill level they have** -- this changes the recommendation more than people expect

### 3. The recommendation

One general assistant, plus at most two specialists. For each: which tasks it covers, and why it rather than the alternatives.

Do not recommend all seven tools. A recommendation that tells people to use everything is not a recommendation.

Avoid quoting prices, limits or feature lists as facts. Say what to check and where.

### 4. The evidence

The section that makes this a recommendation rather than an opinion.

Report your testing: which tools, which tasks, how many inputs, what criteria, what the results were. **Minimum three real inputs across at least two tools.** Reuse and extend the lab.

Include one worked example in full -- the prompt, each tool's output, your marking -- so a reader can check your judgement.

### 5. The rules of use

Three to five rules the group should follow. This section is what separates a useful document from a list of links.

Each rule needs a reason. Good ones tend to cover:

- What must never be pasted into a tool, and why
- What must be verified before it is used, and by whom
- When two tools should be used instead of one
- What has to be disclosed when AI was used
- What the group should not use AI for at all

### 6. How to start

A first week. What to set up, what to try first, what to check after. Concrete enough that someone could follow it on Monday.

## Rubric

Marked out of 100.

**Group and tasks, 15 marks.** Full marks for a named group with four or five specific, genuinely recurring tasks. Marks lost for vague tasks, and for tasks the group does not actually do.

**Constraints, 15 marks.** Full marks where all four are present with a real basis -- an actual policy, an actual data type, an actual budget. Marks lost for constraints asserted without grounding, especially data-sensitivity claims with nothing behind them.

**Recommendation, 20 marks.** Full marks for a focused recommendation -- one general assistant plus at most two specialists -- where each choice is tied to a task and a constraint. Marks lost for recommending everything, and for stale specifics stated as fact.

**Evidence, 25 marks.** Full marks for at least three real inputs across two tools, stated criteria, results as numbers, and one fully worked example. This is the heaviest section. A recommendation with no testing cannot score above half overall.

**Rules of use, 15 marks.** Full marks for three to five specific rules, each with a reason, including at least one thing the group should not use AI for. Marks lost for rules that restate the obvious, such as "check the output".

**How to start, 10 marks.** Full marks for a first week someone could actually follow. Marks lost for a list of links.

## What will cost you marks

**Recommending tools you did not test.** The evidence section must cover what you recommend. Recommending a tool you could not access is fine if you say so and explain what you would test.

**A document with no "do not use it for this" rule.** Every honest recommendation has one. Its absence suggests you have not thought about where the group could get hurt.

**Writing for a marker instead of the group.** If your document would not survive contact with the actual people, it is not a recommendation. Plain language, no course jargon, no explaining what an LLM is to people who did not ask.

**Quoting figures that expire.** Prices, limits, tiers and feature lists. Say what to check.

:::hint The group I picked has a policy that blocks everything
That is a real and very common situation, and it makes for a strong submission rather than a blocked one. Write the recommendation the constraint actually allows: what can be done with tools already approved, what a request to IT would need to contain, and what the group should not attempt in the meantime. A document that takes the constraint seriously is worth more than one that assumes it away.
:::

lessons.title: Level 1 exam: GenAI Fundamentals
lessons.description: Twenty questions and two applied tasks covering modules 1 to 5.
lessons.content:
This is the **Level 1 certification exam: GenAI Fundamentals**. It covers modules 1 to 5.

## Before you start

**Sit it in one go**, without notes and without an AI tool open. The point is to find out what you know, and a score you obtained with help tells you nothing useful.

Twenty questions. Expect it to take about forty minutes.

The questions are harder than the module practice questions and several draw on more than one module. That is deliberate: understanding how tokens, context and hallucination connect is the thing this level certifies.

**Pass mark: 14 out of 20.**

:::quiz
Q. A colleague says the AI "learned from our conversation yesterday and remembered it today". What is actually happening?
- The model fine-tuned itself on the conversation
- The conversation was added to its training data
+ Nothing carried over; if it appears to remember, the transcript was re-sent or a memory feature retrieved it
- The model stored it in its context window permanently
= Training and inference are separate. During inference the weights are frozen. Apparent memory is either the transcript being re-read, or a stored note being retrieved and put into the prompt -- neither of which changes the model.

Q. You paste a 40-page report and ask a question about page 2. The answer ignores it. What is the most likely cause?
- The model cannot read PDFs
+ The report filled the context window and the earliest material was dropped or poorly attended to
- The model has a knowledge cutoff before the report was written
- The question was ambiguous
= Everything competes for the same context window, and even within it a detail buried in a long input is less likely to be used than one near the end. Point at the section that matters rather than trusting it was noticed.

Q. Which pair of tasks carries the *lowest* hallucination risk?
- Listing five papers on a topic, and stating a company's current revenue
- Explaining a historical event, and giving a drug interaction
+ Summarising a document you pasted, and rewriting a paragraph you wrote
- Naming the author of a book, and quoting a statute
= Both are transformation of material in front of the model. The others are recall, which is where invention clusters. This distinction is the single most useful one in the first half of the course.

Q. A model produces a confident, detailed answer about a committee report that does not exist. Which description is accurate?
- The model was trained on unreliable sources about that committee
+ A plausible continuation existed for that sentence shape, and nothing in the system checks whether it is true
- The model confused it with a real report
- The model's knowledge cutoff caused it to guess
= There is no truth-checking mechanism to fail. The model produced likely text. Plausible and true overlap heavily, which is why the tools are useful and why this failure looks identical to a correct answer.

Q. Why is counting the letter "r" in "strawberry" harder for a model than it looks?
- The word is rare in training data
+ The model never saw the letters; it saw two or three tokens
- Counting requires arithmetic, which models cannot do
- The model processes words in parallel, losing order
= Tokenization explains a whole family of odd behaviour. A task that is trivial for a person can be genuinely awkward for a system that never sees characters.

Q. Two sentences share no words but mean nearly the same thing. What makes a system rank them as similar?
- Tokenization
- The attention mechanism
+ Their embeddings landing close together
- A larger context window
= This is why semantic search finds text that means the right thing rather than text that uses the right words, and it is the foundation of retrieval later in the course.

Q. What does the attention mechanism let a model do that earlier designs did badly?
- Process longer inputs in less memory
+ Work out, for each word, which other words in the passage matter for it -- including words that come later
- Remember previous conversations
- Generate several tokens at once
= "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big" versus "too small". One word at the end decides what a pronoun in the middle refers to. A model reading strictly left to right handles that badly.

Q. Doubling the length of an input roughly multiplies the attention work by how much?
- Two
+ Four
- Eight
- It stays the same
= The cost grows roughly with the square of the length, because every position is compared with every other. This is the main reason context windows have limits and why long inputs cost disproportionately more.

Q. Which statement about parameters and context windows is correct?
- Both are set per request
+ Parameters are permanent learned capacity; the context window is temporary visible text
- Parameters determine how much text the model can read at once
- A larger context window means more parameters
= Parameters are what the model learned once during training and never change while you use it. The context window is emptied every conversation.

Q. An organisation handles patient records and wants AI help summarising them. The records cannot leave their systems. What follows?
- Use the most capable proprietary model and accept the risk
+ They are choosing among models they can run themselves, and the capability gap is a cost they accept
- Anonymise the records and use any tool
- Cost becomes the deciding factor
= Data sensitivity can end the decision on its own, before capability or cost are considered. Anonymisation may help but is not automatic, and "can this data leave the building" is the first question.

Q. What is usually wrong with describing Llama as "open source"?
- It is not free to use
+ The trained weights are published, but the training data and code generally are not
- It requires a commercial licence for all use
- Its weights cannot be downloaded
= "Open weights" is the honest term. You get the result of training, not the means to reproduce it, and several such models carry licences restricting commercial use.

Q. You need to choose between a small cheap model and a large expensive one for classifying support emails. What should you do first?
- Compare their benchmark scores
- Choose the larger one, since accuracy matters
+ Label fifty real emails by hand, then run both against them
- Choose based on context window size
= Without labelled examples you are comparing impressions. An hour of labelling turns an unanswerable question into an easy one, and it very often shows the small model is good enough.

Q. A multimodal model reads a chart from a screenshot. Which output should you trust least?
- A description of the overall trend
- Identifying what the axes represent
+ A specific value read off the chart
- Naming the chart type
= Excellent at meaning, unreliable at precision. It will describe a trend well and misread a number confidently. Never take a figure off a chart without checking it against the underlying data.

Q. Which change to a prompt typically has the largest effect on output quality?
- Adding "please" and "thank you"
- Claiming the model is an expert
+ Supplying the source material instead of relying on recall
- Making the prompt longer
= Missing context is the most common cause of disappointing output. People know their own situation so well they forget the model knows only what was typed.

Q. You have described a tone in four paragraphs and the output still misses it. What should you do?
- Describe it in more detail
+ Show two or three examples of the tone instead
- Claim a role that would produce that tone
- Ask the model to try harder
= It is far easier to demonstrate a tone than to describe one. Few-shot examples make your pattern the obvious continuation, which is why they succeed where instructions fail.

Q. What does "You are a senior cardiologist" actually change?
- The model's medical knowledge
- The accuracy of medical claims
+ The vocabulary, register and perspective of the output
- The model's willingness to say it is unsure
= A role shifts which region of language the output is drawn from. It adds no knowledge and no reliability, and it can make a wrong answer sound more authoritative -- which is worse than useless.

Q. Which single line does most to stop a structured extraction inventing values?
- "Return only valid JSON"
- "You are a careful data analyst"
+ "If a field is not stated, use null. Do not infer."
- "Be accurate"
= Without it, a missing field gets a plausible invented value. That is harder to catch than ordinary hallucination because the JSON parses perfectly and the value looks extracted rather than generated.

Q. You changed five things in a prompt and the output improved. What is the problem?
- Nothing; the prompt is now better
+ You cannot tell which change helped, which did nothing, and which hurt
- The prompt is now too long
- The improvement may not be reproducible
= Changing one thing per round feels slower and is faster, because you end with a prompt where every clause earns its place and you know why it is there.

Q. When should evaluation criteria be written?
- After seeing the first output, so they are realistic
+ Before running anything, against the task
- After comparing two prompt versions
- Only when the prompt is finished
= Criteria written after seeing output are unconsciously shaped to what the output happened to do. If output later reveals a criterion you missed, add it and re-mark every version, including ones already scored.

Q. A search-first tool answers a contested question fluently with five citations. What is the correct response?
- Accept it; five citations is strong corroboration
- Check whether the model has a recent cutoff
+ Click the sources and judge them, since a synthesis can flatten real disagreement into false consensus
- Ask the same question again to check consistency
= You have outsourced source evaluation and the only way to see how it went is to look. A fluent answer over weak sources is worse than no answer, because it is convincing.
:::

## The applied section

Answer both. Together they are worth as much as the twenty questions.

### Task 1: diagnose a prompt

A colleague sends you this and says the output is "generic and too long":

> You are an expert business analyst. Write a report on our Q3 performance. Don't make it too long or use too much jargon. Make it good.

Identify **four** specific faults, naming the part of a prompt each one is missing or misusing. Then rewrite it. You may invent the context you need, but state what you invented.

### Task 2: sort by risk

For each of these, say whether you would use a general assistant, use it with verification, use it only for thinking, or not use it at all -- with a one-line reason:

1. Summarising a meeting transcript you recorded
2. Finding three academic sources on a topic for an essay
3. Drafting a condolence message to a colleague
4. Deciding which of two job candidates to shortlist
5. Explaining a concept from a lecture you did not follow

## Marking

**The questions: 20 marks**, one each. Pass is 14.

**Task 1: 12 marks.** Three per fault correctly identified and named. Full marks require naming the missing part -- context, constraints, format, and an empty expertise claim -- not just saying it is vague. The rewrite must supply context, audience, length, format and an uncertainty instruction.

**Task 2: 8 marks.** Roughly: 1 is safe transformation; 2 needs a search-first tool and full verification, never a general assistant from recall; 3 should not be AI-assisted because being you is the point; 4 is never -- it evaluates a person; 5 is one of the strongest uses. Marks are for the reasoning, not the label alone.

**Total: 40 marks. Pass: 28.**

## If you do not pass

Nothing is lost. Look at which questions you missed and go back to those lessons rather than resitting immediately.

The most common weak areas are the mechanism questions -- tokens, context, attention, why hallucination happens -- because they are the ones people skim. They are also the ones everything in Level 2 builds on.
